statement_pretty:
∀ {α : Type} [inst_2 : DecidableEq α] [inst_3 : Fintype α] {f : Equiv.Perm α}
  {l : List (Equiv.Perm α)},
  f ∈ l →
    List.Pairwise Equiv.Perm.Disjoint l →
      ∀ {u v : Equiv.Perm α},
        l.prod.Disjoint u → v.support ⊆ u.support → f.support ≠ ⊥ → ¬IsMax v.support

referees.justification: Calibrated zero-token rubric evaluation assigns an expected importance of 4.53/10 (confidence 0.25) and classifies the result as a Lemma (p = 0.44) in MSC 20-XX. Independent probability estimates yield P(surprising) = 0.15 and P(a human mathematician cares) = 0.20.

The result merely observes that a permutation whose support is disjoint from that of a nontrivial member of a pairwise disjoint list cannot have maximal support, which is an immediate consequence of basic set-theoretic disjointness. The proliferation of auxiliary permutations and list-product hypotheses lends an air of generality to what is essentially a routine bookkeeping lemma.

editorial.title: Lemma on Non-Maximality of Disjoint-Product Support Inclusions

editorial.unverified_gloss:
For a finite type α, let f be a non-identity permutation belonging to a list l of pairwise disjoint permutations of α. If u and v are permutations of α such that u is disjoint from the product of l and v.support ⊆ u.support, then v.support is not maximal in Finset α (i.e., v does not move every element of α).

In essence, the hypotheses on f and l merely ensure that f.support is a nonempty subset of the support of l.prod, which is disjoint from u.support and therefore from v.support—forcing v.support to be a proper subset of α.
